newsitem.title: USA: Genzyme gains on new Phase 3 Thyrogen data.
newsitem.headline: Genzyme gains on new Phase 3 Thyrogen data.

text.p: Genzyme Corp shares gained Thursday on enthusiasm over results of a second Phase III trial of the company's Thyrogen thyroid stimulating hormone, analysts said.

Genzyme late Wednesday said Thyrogen produced radioiodine scans clinically and statistically equivalent to those produced after patients were taken off their thyroid hormone supplements prior to undergoing such scans.
Radioidine scans are used to test for recurrence of cancer following partial or total surgical removal of cancerous thyroid glands and follow-up treatment.

The company said the new data showed improved results over an earlier Phase III study completed in 1994, adding it intended to file a new drug application for Thyrogen later this year with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Genzyme shares gained 1-3/4 to 24-1/2 in afternoon trading, boosted by the test results and company estimates Thyrogen had a market potential of $75 million in the U.S., Canada and Europe.

"If all goes well, the drug will probably bring in about $30 million to $40 million a year," said Mehta and Isaly drug analyst Edmund Debler, who described it as a small sum compared with his projections of total company revenue of $640 million in 1997.
"But people are looking for a reason to buy the stock," he said, following its moderate decline in recent months.
After removal of their thyroid glands, patients must take a synthetic thyroid hormone supplement daily to replace the hormones normally produced by the gland.

But weeks before undergoing scanning, patients must stop taking the supplement in order to prod their bodies into resuming production of naturally occuring Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (THS) -- which is needed to absorb and retain iodine that is measured in the test.
Meanwhile, however, patients begin to develop fatigue, depression and other symptoms of hypothyroidism because of withdrawal from the synthetic hormone replacement.

Thyrogen provides an alternate method of raising a patient's TSH level prior to testing while allowing patients to continue taking their thyroid hormone supplement, thus avoiding the symptoms of hypothyroidism, the company said.
Investigators from 11 U.S. and three European medical centers tested 220 patients in the second Phase III trial, Genzyme said.
It said data showed Thyrogen produced scans that were equivalent to scans produced after withdrawing patients from thyroid hormone supplements in over 90 percent of patients.
